beats.text: Food safety starts with effective cleaning. Detergent at the right strength helps remove food residues and biofilm. On the cleaned surface, sanitiser is then used for the required kill step, at the approved concentration and contact time. Chemical concentration verification — CCV — checks that each solution is within its approved range.

This is where a supervisor actually meets it. Not on a chemistry screen — on the day's certificate. A coral strip at the top of the Bill of Health, and it names them: Argonox at Satellite seven, four days past its window. Alkafoam at Crate washer one, three days. Argonox at Satellite five, two days. Three dosing points nobody has verified. The certificate tells you before an auditor does.

Tap it and you land on the Chemical hub. Three numbers first: five due, two done, none out of spec. Then the band that matters — periodic verification due. The same three dosing points, with the days since anyone last verified them. Eighteen. Seventeen. Sixteen. Below that, today's activity: twenty-one issued, twenty-one verified, twenty-one passed. The hub is activity first. The strip is the exception.

beats.chip: + issue → Verify now / later → Awaiting verification
beats.text: Issuing starts with the plus. Pick the station. Then complete the form: the batch or lot number, the scope, issue type and quantities. For manual dilution, enter both chemical and water; the app calculates the percentage against the approved range. Record the issue. For a manual dilution, normally choose Verify now. Verify later leaves the check pending. For satellites and dosing stations, you can return to verification later. On the Chemical hub, open Awaiting verification. It includes issues from earlier days. Find the issue and tap Verify to continue its check.

Now verification. The approved range is already waiting — nought point three to two percent — and the selected method is titration drops. The operator does not choose either. Tap How to test. The reagents are listed. The procedure is step by step. The calculation is drops times nought point nought nine five. Follow the work instruction. For this method, enter both the drop count and the percentage it gives.

Conductivity has one extra step. Plant water is not the same at every site, or every day. So once a shift, before the first check, you measure the tap water and set the baseline. Every conductivity reading that shift is corrected against it. Skip it, and the app blocks the reading until you do. One measurement, once. Then the rest of the shift just flows.

Most days it is this simple. Follow the drop procedure and enter twenty drops. Enter the reading — one point nine percent. In spec. The verdict is the entered reading against the approved range, not the operator's opinion. Record it, and that dosing point is verified for the cadence.

Forty drops. Three point eight percent. Out of spec. Two things appear, and both are required before recording: corrective action and a re-test reading. In What you did, record the action taken. Then repeat the method: enter twenty drops and one point nine percent. If the re-test passes, the record keeps both the miss and the recovery. That is the second pair of eyes doing its job.

What if the re-test fails too? One operator shouldn't carry that alone. So the app raises a non-conformance and names the site manager. The button becomes Record and Escalate. On their own device, the manager acknowledges, and signs. Accountability travels up the chain — automatically.

beats.chip: History rows · detail · back on the hub
beats.text: And it is all there afterwards. Every issue on the hub: who issued it, which department, how much. Under it, the verification — the method, the reading, pass or fail, and the name. Open the detail and it is the same record, with the time it was made. Not a percentage somebody typed in later. A reading taken at the station, when the work was done. Back on the hub: none out of spec. That is what an auditor gets to see.

Factory floors have dead spots. CCV doesn't care. Offline, every action saves instantly — with a buzz — then waits in a queue. When the signal returns, they run like a relay, in strict order. Temporary IDs are swapped for real ones. And a retry that tries to submit twice is turned away. Nothing lost. Nothing doubled.

Three things to hold onto. The certificate tells you first. The standard is already set before anyone touches a station. And every reading is measured, not assumed — recorded at the time, by the person who did it. Fail, and the app walks you through re-test and escalation. A second pair of eyes on every drum. One that never blinks first.
